doc.title: Luther Henderson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Night Creature for Don Gillis at Carnegie Hall
summary: In 1955 he orchestrated Duke's Night Creature for the Symphony of the Air, working from taped sketches made while following Ellington on tour.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Now tell me about the creation and the subsequent broadcast of “Night Creature” for the Symphony of the Air and your part in that.
Well this was, what year was that … 1955.

Okay. Now I had been a few years away from Lena Horne because I was with her in late '40s, maybe '50s, something like that. Anyway, the Symphony of the Air, Don Gillis had, I don't know, been commissioned that he was to do these works which he was already doing with his band. I don't know if he was doing Night Creature. I think Night Creature may have been done specifically for that concert. But at any rate, and he wanted to perform it at Carnegie Hall with a, in a symphony setting. And this is when he called me and I guess that would have been … it was done in 1955 so … I don't know, I didn't have a whole lot of time to do it, you know, because … but the point is that what I did was to follow him around the country wherever I could find … in other words, he didn't do like we do, you know, you sit down and okay we're gonna have a session, we're gonna write some music and so forth. No, no, you'd go and you'd follow him to whatever

his band thing was, where he was gonna play that night, and then after the gig is over, you go and get something to eat and somehow he would stay up and he would talk and play .. I have some little cassettes about how he would instruct us, what he wanted to do and stuff like that. So it came like that. And the, all three things were … I had sketches and if I'm not mistaken, some spot tapes that he would take on the dates. I have to remember exactly how did I get all because it was very
He would record ideas for you?

Well you know when he would do it on a, at a night club for instance and someone would be there with a tape. This was, you know we were past wire recording. We did have tapes at this time. Somebody put it on a tape. Also some of these things have been recorded just with his own orchestra, if I'm not mistaken, with the orchestra alone, without the symphony. So that may be how we got hold of a lot of this stuff.
But in any event you had a recorded framework to work from?
Which made the transposition or ideas a lot easier
